extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a claimed invention is patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the MPEP two-step analysis (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: judicial exceptions and inventive concept). Applies to examination of claims for subject matter eligibility and related procedural handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for 35 U.S.C. 101 eligibility (two-step test)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 and both must be satisfied. The claimed invention (1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories, and (2) must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The following two step analysis is used to evaluate these criteria (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: judicial exceptions). Both criteria must be satisfied for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Directed to a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Is the claim directed to one of the four patent-eligible subject matter categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter? The subject matter of the claim must be directed to one of the four subject matter categories. If it is not, the claim is not eligible for patent protection and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed invention is clearly not within one of the four categories, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made. However, when the claim fails under Step 1 and it appears the claim could be amended to be directed to a statutory category, Step 2 should still be conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Process – an act, or a series of acts or steps. (Cites Gottschalk v. Benson: 'A process is a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result. It is an act, or a series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also 35 U.S.C. 100(b) and cases such as Bilski v. Kappos and NTP, Inc. v. Research in Motion for related precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine – a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices. This includes every mechanical device or combination of mechanical powers and devices to perform some function and produce a certain effect or result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Burr v. Duryee and Corning v. Burden as authorities describing machines as concrete devices or combinations of devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacture – an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations, whether by hand labor or by machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Diamond v. Chakrabarty and Am. Fruit Growers, Inc. v. Brogdex Co. as definitional authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Composition of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of matter – all compositions of two or more substances and all composite articles, whether the results of chemical union, mechanical mixture, or whether gases, fluids, powders or solids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Chakrabarty as authority; applies to chemical/biological compositions and composite articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting examples of non-statutory subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories include: transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se); a human per se; a legal contractual agreement between two parties; a computer program per se; a company; a mere arrangement of printed matter; and data per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each example is supported by case law citations (e.g., In re Nuijten; AIA; In re Ferguson; Gottschalk v. Benson; In re Miller; Digitech Image Tech.). Use these examples when assessing whether a claim falls outside the statutory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth that includes non-statutory embodiments (Step 1 failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification and a person skilled in the art) embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media that can be a carrier wave), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 as failing to claim statutory subject matter is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2: Does the claim wholly embrace a judicially recognized exception, which includes laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas? Determining that a claim falls within one of the four categories does not end the eligibility analysis because claims directed to nothing more than abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature are not eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial exceptions have been described using various other terms, including 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles,' 'systems that depend on human intelligence alone,' 'disembodied concepts,' 'mental processes,' and 'disembodied mathematical algorithms and formulas.' See Alice, Myriad, Bilski and related cases for application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis for claims directed to judicial exceptions — 'significantly more' / inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether the elements of the claim, considered both individually and as an ordered combination, are sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception itself—this is a search for an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claim as a whole is for a particular application of an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature, as opposed to the abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature itself. See Alice, Mayo, and Diehr for the courts' framework and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions — policy rationale and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The exceptions reflect the courts’ view that the basic tools of scientific and technological work (principles, fundamental truths, natural phenomena, mathematical formulas) are not patentable; e.g., a new mineral discovered in the earth or a new plant found in the wild is not patentable subject matter; nor can one patent a mathematical formula or law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cited cases (Le Roy v. Tatham; Funk Bros.; Chakrabarty; Flook; O’Reilly v. Morse) to explain the policy basis that manifestations of laws of nature are part of the storehouse of knowledge and free to all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish on the record a prima facie case (examiner burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (e.g., the specification, claims, relevant prior art) before reaching a conclusion. USPTO personnel must reach a conclusion as to whether it is more likely than not that the claimed invention as a whole either falls outside of one of the enumerated statutory classes or within one of the exceptions to statutory subject matter. 'The examiner bears the initial burden … of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record as a whole suggests it is more likely than not that the claimed invention would be considered significantly more than an exception, then USPTO personnel should not reject the claim. After USPTO personnel identify and explain why a claim is for an exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend the claim or show eligibility (e.g., In re Brana).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural guidance — compact prosecution and stating non-cumulative reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the principles of compact prosecution, regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made based on lack of subject matter eligibility, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each of the other patentability requirements: 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and utility/inventorship/double patenting issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural action when claim fails Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention is clearly not within one of the four categories, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating that the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 should be used; see MPEP § 706.03(a). Nonetheless, if the claim could be amended to be directed to a statutory category, Step 2 analysis should still be performed.
